defects: Image does not support a sufficiently distinct teaching answer: The visible lesion is an expansile lytic lesion with lobulated contour and internal chondroid/ground-glass matrix density in the proximal phalanx of the middle finger of a skeletally immature hand. This appearance is most consistent with enchondroma radiographically. Tuberculous dactylitis (spina ventosa) classically produces a fusiform, ballooned, lucent proximal phalanx with periosteal reaction and soft tissue swelling but without internal matrix calcification or chondroid density. The internal ground-glass/chondroid matrix visible here strongly favors enchondroma over TB dactylitis. The clinical vignette (slow swelling over months in a young child) is compatible with either, but the radiographic matrix density is the discriminating visible feature and it does not favor TB dactylitis. Another diagnosis (enchondroma) is equally or better supported by the visible radiographic pattern, so singleAnswerSupported is false.

findings: PA projection of a single hand, fingers extended and slightly spread
Skeletally immature hand with visible epiphyseal growth plates at the distal, middle, and proximal phalanges and metacarpal bases/heads; physes appear open throughout

Large, well-defined, expansile lytic lesion with endosteal scalloping involving the proximal phalanx of the long (middle) finger; the lesion occupies the majority of the medullary canal, has a lobulated contour, and demonstrates internal ground-glass or chondroid matrix density; cortex appears thinned but intact
No acute fracture line visible through the lesion
Remaining phalanges and metacarpals appear normal in density and contour
Carpal bones partially visible at the distal margin; no obvious carpal abnormality
Soft tissues appear unremarkable except for mild fusiform swelling overlying the affected proximal phalanx
differential: Enchondroma of the proximal phalanx of the middle finger (most common benign intramedullary cartilage tumor at this site in a skeletally immature patient)
Ollier disease (enchondromatosis) — solitary lesion here but multiple enchondromas cannot be excluded without full skeletal survey
Low-grade chondrosarcoma (less likely given patient skeletal immaturity and benign radiographic margins, but cannot be entirely excluded for an expansile lesion of this size)
anatomyConcerns: Open physes throughout indicate a skeletally immature individual; the expansile lytic lesion in the proximal phalanx is a true pathological finding, not a normal variant
No significant acquisition or positioning inconsistencies identified; the projection is standard PA hand
